clinician.trajectory_summary: A 41-year-old man presented with worsening headache, nausea, and photophobia. Initial blood tests and head CT were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed CSF findings consistent with viral meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, normal glucose). CSF PCR subsequently detected VZV DNA, confirming VZV meningitis. The patient also had a history of rashes with blisters on his nose and hard palate, consistent with herpes zoster reactivation, which he experienced before his visit. He was treated with intravenous acyclovir for 14 days, leading to improvement of his symptoms.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with worsening headache, nausea, and photophobia for 3 days.
Initial blood tests and head CT were unremarkable.
CSF analysis showed an initial pressure of 16 cm H2O, leucocyte count of 217/μL (92% lymphocytes), protein level of 129 mg/dL, and glucose level of 55 mg/dL (blood glucose level of 138 mg/dL).
CSF tested positive for VZV DNA via PCR.
Rashes with blisters were observed on the left side of his nose and hard palate in the area of the second branch of the trigeminal nerve, which the patient experienced before his visit.
He received intravenous acyclovir for 14 days, resulting in improvement of symptoms.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose, which are atypical for bacterial meningitis. The positive VZV PCR further supports a viral etiology.
While not explicitly ruled out by negative PCRs, the positive VZV DNA in CSF and the characteristic VZV rash strongly point to VZV as the causative agent.

remaining_uncertainties: Explicit negative results for other CSF pathogens (e.g., bacterial cultures, HSV PCR, enterovirus PCR) were not documented.
Long-term clinical outcome beyond symptom improvement.
